80	# The anti-slop catalogue
81	
82	Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.
83	
84	The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.
85	
86	## The test before a pattern is recorded
87	
88	Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.
89	
90	The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.
91	
92	Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.
93	
94	## The seven patterns
95	
96	**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.
97	
98	**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.
99	
100	**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.
101	
102	**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.
103	
104	**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.
105	
106	**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.
107	
108	**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

138	# Craft for five web genres
139	
140	For article, casestudy, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For webcopy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.
141	
142	In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.
143	
144	## Web reading
145	
146	Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.
147	
148	For article, casestudy, column and opinion, the [article anatomy](article-anatomy.md) fixes the parts, their order and their dimensions.
149	=== web-craft.review.md
150	# Reviewing web craft
151	
152	Read under [the craft brief](web-craft.md). Test the text as a reader who scans, then as one who follows its reasoning. Identify the actual cost of a dense or fragmented passage before proposing a change.
153	
154	Distinguish target-language fluency from editorial tradition. A Swedish angle expressed in natural English succeeds; Swedish word order in English does not. Equally, flawless local spelling does not rescue generic promotional prose from a lost journalistic purpose. Preserve successful genre-specific voice and structure instead of standardising them.
155	=== article-anatomy.md
156	# Article anatomy
157	
158	The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.
159	
160	A statement below has one of three strengths:
161	
162	- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
163	- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
164	- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.
165	
166	A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.
167	
168	A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.
169	
170	## Order
171	
172	```text
173	Headline
174	Standfirst
175	Byline
176	Lead
177	Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
178	Paragraphs        ┘
179	Last subheading   ┐ the ending
180	Paragraphs        ┘
181	```
182	
183	Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.
184	
185	The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.
186	
187	## Headline
188	
189	- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
190	- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
191	- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
192	
193	## Standfirst
194	
195	The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.
196	
197	- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
198	- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
199	- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
200	- It entices the reader to read on.
201	
202	## Byline
203	
204	One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.
205	
206	## Lead
207	
208	The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.
209	
210	### Standfirst and lead
211	
212	Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:
213	
214	- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
215	- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
216	- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.
217	
218	## Paragraphs
219	
220	- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
221	- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
222	- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
223	- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.
224	
225	## Subheadings and sections
226	
227	A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.
228	
229	- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
230	- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
231	- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.
232	
233	## Ending
234	
235	The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:
236	
237	- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
238	- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.
239	
240	The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
241	=== article-anatomy.review.md
242	# Article anatomy — review guidance
243	
244	Read under [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md), and word each finding in the strength the statement it rests on has.
245	
246	A requirement that fails is a finding. Count characters and words before reporting a limit, and give the count.
247	
248	A part the text does not have is reported, and a part it has is repaired. Where a required part is absent — the headline, the standfirst, the byline, the lead, a section, or the ending with its call to action — its absence is a finding, and the part is not written: not from the text's own content and not from anywhere else, since the text is finished and a person decides what fills it. A part the text has that fails its own rule is repaired like any other defect, from the text's own content. A part in the wrong place is present, not absent, and is repaired by moving it into place: a byline standing at the end of the text is moved to its place in the order, although the measuring script reports the byline `absent`. Ending content the text has — closing paragraphs that show the lead's expectation met or call the reader to act — is a present ending. Where the last section is an ending by the anatomy's test, a defect in it, a vague call to action among them, is repaired where it stands from what the text already says. Where the closing content stands inside a last section that carries the argument, or inside a text's only section, it is a present ending that fails its rule, since the ending is a section of its own: it is repaired by giving it a section of its own, opened by its own subheading and built from the text's own content, the closing content moving there and a vague call to action among it repaired from what the text already says. At the close of a text with no section at all, closing content is repaired where it stands from what the text already says, and no section and no subheading is written to hold it: the text has no ending section either, and that is reported with its absent sections. A text with no ending content at all has an absent ending, and a text that calls the reader to no action has an absent call to action; both are reported. A failure the script reports only because another part is absent is reported as that absent part and is not repaired by writing it: a lead of several paragraphs in a text with no subheading fails only because its sections are absent, so the finding is the absent sections, and no section and no subheading is written to make the lead one paragraph. Likewise a text of one section with no ending content fails the section count only because its ending is absent, and the finding is the absent ending. Where the script takes the text's one opening paragraph as its standfirst and reports the lead absent, whichever of the two that paragraph is taken for, the other is absent and is reported.
249	
250	A departure from a *should* is a finding only when following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it. A paragraph a little past the edge that holds one thought and reads well at that length has met the bar. A paragraph far past it, or paragraphs that run long throughout, cost the web reader something a finding can name. The anatomy's bands are its four *should* norms on a dimension, each with the figure [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md) gives it: the headline's word norm and its character norm, a paragraph's word norm, and a section's paragraph norm. A band is not by itself a defect. A headline, a subheading or a paragraph the text has that meets its requirements is not rewritten, split or merged only to come inside a band. A change the test above justifies is not made only to come inside one: it repairs what the finding names the reader losing, as a split of a paragraph far past the edge does. The limits the script reports as failures are requirements, not bands — the headline's character limits, a subheading's maximum, and the standfirst's single paragraph and its word limit, each as the anatomy states it — and a part that fails one is repaired. A subheading has no band, only its maximum. A subheading that describes clearly what its section is about meets its requirement, and is not rewritten from a label into a statement on that ground alone; one that does not describe its section fails that requirement and is repaired.
251	
252	*Most* is read across the whole text, and no single paragraph or section fails it. A four-sentence paragraph is no finding. A paragraph holding two thoughts is one, and so is a text whose paragraphs are nearly all a single sentence or nearly all long. Name the pattern and what it costs the reader rather than the count.
253	
254	Read the standfirst separately, then with the lead. Can it introduce the piece on its own, and does the lead start doing the promised work? Repeated orientation may be necessary; an opening that restarts without advancing is the defect. Then read the body with the standfirst covered. A pronoun, a definite form or a phrase such as *the reason* whose referent only the standfirst supplies is a finding, repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it.
255	
256	In a text under review, the author is whoever the text, its metadata or the invocation names. A byline nobody can name is reported as missing and left unfilled: the reviewer's user is not presumed to have written a text they brought for review.
257	=== headlines.md
258	# Headlines
259	
260	How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.
261	
262	## Statement or label
263	
264	A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.
265	
266	## What a statement headline does
267	
268	- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
269	- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
270	- The most important keyword comes first.
271	- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
272	- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
273	- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
274	- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
275	- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
276	- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
277	- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
278	- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
279	- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
280	- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.
281	
282	## Every word supported
283	
284	A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.
285	
286	## A subheading over a quotation
287	
288	A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.
289	
290	The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.
291	
292	## Getting there
293	
294	Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
295	=== headlines.review.md
296	# Headlines — review guidance
297	
298	Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?
299	
300	## Avoid
301	
302	Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding where you can name what a reader of that heading loses, and no finding where you cannot. A reader loses something where the heading claims more than the text, or something other than it; is louder in tone than the text; says again, in substance, what stands under it; gives away the point of a quotation under it; is a bare label or subject where the text has an angle, or a question where the text answers it; uses words the audience does not know; or leaves a reader who sees only the heading unable to tell what the text is about. Those are instances of the test and not the whole of it, so an item they do not name is still a finding wherever the test holds, as where a colon in place of a verb leaves the reader unable to tell who did what. A loss is something the reader gets wrong or does not get: what the text claims, how seriously it speaks, what it is about, a quotation's point met fresh. A heading that could be clearer, more specific, more complete or closer to the angle you would have chosen loses its reader nothing, and on a finished text it is left as it is:
303	
304	- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
305	- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
306	- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
307	- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
308	- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
309	- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
310	- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
311	- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
312	- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
313	- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. Read it against the quotation however far down the section the quotation stands. Repair it by naming the subject, the occasion or the speaker, or by stating what the rest of the section says, and leave the quotation as it is.
314	
315	Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is. A headline or a subheading a round changed is reported with this finding — the part, and the defect that licensed the change — and, where the new one asserts something the old did not, with what it now asserts, so that a reader of the account can tell a repaired part from a rewritten one. A repair keeps the text's recurring words and figures and its meaning: a word or an image the text returns to comes back in the form the text gives it, and the heading names the text's point in the text's own word for it, never in a neighbouring word that widens or shifts what the text says.
316	
317	## Leave alone
318	
319	A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label.
320	
321	Read a heading as its reader meets it, and count a loss that reader would suffer, not one that the strictest reading of a single word could construct. A reader who sees only the heading, as a headline in a list or a search result, has nothing else, so a headline alone has to tell that reader what the text is about. A subheading is met after the headline and the standfirst, so a word or a name they have introduced is known to its reader, and a subheading that refers back to one is not unclear. Four kinds of heading are working, and no *Avoid* item makes one a finding by its wording alone. None of the four overrides the first *Avoid* item, a claim the text does not support as a reader would take it, or the item on a subheading that pre-spends a quotation standing under it:
322	
323	- An allusion or an image that still tells a reader who sees only the heading what the text is about. It names the text's subject, and may name it in general terms where the text's first lines give the particulars. One that names no subject at all leaves its reader unable to tell what the text is about, however soon the body resolves it, and that is a finding.
324	- A figure of speech in the text's own register, or the writer's own voice in a signed text, first person included. A figure is an overclaim only where a reader would take it as a factual claim the text does not support, and there the first *Avoid* item decides; an *everything*, a *nothing* or a *never* that overstates in the way the figure means to is read as the figure it is.
325	- A subheading that states what its section says, where the section's point is not a quotation's judgement, figure or concession. A subheading that sums up its section says what the section says as a whole; that is its work, not a repeat, and it may name the section's limit or its setting rather than its most favourable result. Where the section's point is a quotation's judgement, figure or concession, a subheading that states that point pre-spends the quotation and stays a finding.
326	- A heading that shares names or topic words with the sentence under it while saying something that sentence does not. A repeat is a finding by what it says again, not by the words it shares.
327	
328	Where you would word a working heading differently but can name no loss, record nothing against it: a note that it could be better is not a finding, and it licenses no change.
329	
330	A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.

````markdown
# Behåll telefonbokningen ett halvår och mät tidsåtgången

Sanna Ek, Öppna beslut

Kommunstyrelsen borde behålla telefonbokning under ett halvårs försök i alla sju lokaler.

## Var femte bokning kom via telefon, men unika personer räknades inte

Det gjordes 96 bokningar på webben och 24 via telefon. Det är 20 procent av bokningarna. Kommunens pilotrapport från den 8 april 2026 säger samtidigt att bokningarna inte räknar unika personer och att digital vana inte undersöktes.

## Handlingarna visar inte hur mycket tid två bokningsvägar tar

Förvaltningen invänder att dubbla kanaler innebär dubbel administration. Handlingarna saknar tidsmätning. Föreningen vill att förvaltningen mäter tidsåtgång och frågar användarna varför de väljer en bokningsväg. Försökets kostnad är inte beräknad.

## Kommunstyrelsen och förvaltningen har var sitt steg att ta

Nu är det dags att agera. Kommunstyrelsen kan behålla telefonbokningen under ett halvårs försök i alla sju lokaler. Förvaltningen kan mäta tidsåtgången och fråga användarna.
````

**Repaired**
- **1 (headline):** The headline no longer claims that "kommunledningen" hates people. It now asks for two things: keep phone booking for six months and measure the time it takes. The measuring demand comes from the call in the new ending (finding 8). The headline says "ett halvår" without the word "försök", so the six-month limit is kept.
- **3 (removed as a whole):** I deleted "Alla vet att politikerna vill stänga ute äldre för att spara miljoner." It carried three claims, now gone: that "everyone knows" something, that politicians want to shut out older people, and that this is meant to save millions.
- **4 (changed claim):** "Det bevisar att 20 procent av kommunens invånare inte kan använda internet" now reads "Det är 20 procent av bokningarna." The claim moves from proof about residents' internet ability to a share of bookings: 24 of 120. The claim that residents cannot use the internet is gone. The pilot-report sentence that sets the limits is unchanged.
- **5 (removed claim):** I deleted "Därför kostar det ingenting att behålla telefonbokningen." The claim that keeping phone booking costs nothing is gone. "Handlingarna saknar tidsmätning." stays unchanged.
- **7 (subheadings):** Both labels are rewritten.
  - "Bakgrund" now states the section's share and its limit. The share is one booking in five by phone; the limit is that unique persons were not counted.
  - "Diskussion" now states that the documents do not show how much time two booking routes take. This stays tied to the documents and says no more than the text does.
- **8 (ending):** "Nu är det dags att agera." moved into a section of its own, with a new subheading naming kommunstyrelsen and förvaltningen. After it come two concrete calls built from the text:
  - kommunstyrelsen can keep phone booking for a six-month trial in all seven premises (from the lead);
  - förvaltningen can measure the time taken and ask users (from föreningen's demand).
- **Changed attribution (from 8):** The demand that förvaltningen measure and ask users was föreningen's. It now also appears as part of the author's closing call, and in the headline as an imperative. It is phrased as "kan" in the ending, and no new policy or decision is added.

**Left unrepaired**
- **2 (standfirst):** It is missing, and I did not write one, because the anatomy reserves a missing part for a person to supply. This is also the only failure the script reports.
- **6 ("Föreningen"):** The text never says which association this is, and naming it would add a claim. The paragraph is unchanged.
- **9 (figure sources, period, what is booked):** Fixing this needs information the text doesn't have. I did not attribute the figures to the pilot report.

**Measurement:** `article_anatomy.py` exited with 1. Its one failure is the missing standfirst (finding 2), and all other counted limits pass. I read every heading pair by hand:
- The first subheading adds the share and the limit, which are not in the first sentence under it.
- The second and third subheadings share nothing with their first sentences.
- The headline–standfirst pair can't be checked because there is no standfirst. The headline adds the measuring demand, which is not in the lead.

I did not check the anatomy requirements the script doesn't count, such as the lead–standfirst relation, which can't be tested without a standfirst. So I am not reporting the text as fully conforming. The temporary working directories have been removed.

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

Clock times are written *kl. 14.30* or *14:30*; both are current.\n\nCurrency follows the amount: *1 250 kr*, *250 000 SEK*, with a space before the unit.\n\nA sentence-initial connective adverb takes no comma before the finite verb: *Dessutom är det viktigt*, not *Dessutom, är det viktigt*.\n\nAfter a colon, direct speech or a quotation starts with a capital. A closely connected specification or explanation may begin with lowercase even when it is a complete sentence. An unquoted question can similarly stand as an independent utterance with a capital or as an integrated specification with lowercase; both readings can be valid. A colon followed by several sentences takes a capital.\n\nThe Swedish dash is the en dash, and it is spaced wherever it stands inside a line: the sentence-breaking dash in *snabbare – det*, and the parenthetical insertion, which takes a space on each side. A dash opening a line takes a space after it and has nothing before it to space against. The range is the exception and is unspaced, as above. The em dash belongs to English typography, so *snabbare—det* is an error wherever it stands.\n\nQuotation marks are *”…”* — the same right-pointing mark at both ends — so English marks in *“kundresa”* are an error. Quotation inside quotation uses *’…’*.\n\nThe two marks Swedish sets somebody's speech in promise the reader different things, and which of them a text uses is a claim about its source rather than a matter of taste. Wording inside *”…”* is the speaker's own, and the text vouches for it word for word. A speech dash opens the line, is closed by nothing, and claims the content and the meaning as the speaker's while leaving the wording repairable within the boundary the writing Skill works under: *– Det gick fortare än vi trodde, säger hon.* Repaired wording set inside quotation marks is therefore false about the source rather than a typographic slip. Where one speaker carries on into a new paragraph, that paragraph opens with a speech dash of its own.\n\nA simple list takes no serial comma: *teknik, processer och kultur*, not *teknik, processer, och kultur*.\n\nIn running prose, *och* is written out: *Service och support*, not *Service & support*. Preserve an ampersand that belongs to a proper name or quoted matter.\n\nAbbreviations take periods: *t.ex.*, *bl.a.*, *dvs.*, *m.m.*, *osv.*, *ca* without one. The period marks where a word was cut short, which is what decides a form nobody has listed: an abbreviation that stops before the word's end keeps it — *dir.*, *kap.*, *fig.* — and one that carries the word's own last letter takes none, as *dr*, *kr*, *nr*, and *tfn* do. *Ca* is the exception the list is there for: the word is cut short and the form is still settled without a period.\n\nAn initialism that has become an everyday Swedish word is written in lower case and without periods — *vd*, *tv*, *it*, *sms*, *dna*, *bnp*, *brf* — while one that has not stays in capitals: *SEO*, *GDPR*, *EU*. Neither set is closed. What puts an initialism in the first of them is that Swedish has stopped reading it as letters standing for words and reads it as a word of its own — one a reader takes at sight, inflects, and compounds without stopping at what it abbreviates — so a form nobody would need expanded belongs there whether or not it is listed here. An initialism compounded with a word takes a hyphen and keeps whichever case it has on its own: *vd-brev*, *USA-baserad*, *EU-direktiv*.\n\nGenitive takes *s* without an apostrophe, and nothing at all after *s*, *x*, or *z*: *företagets resultat*, *Lars hus*.\n\nOnly the first word of a heading or title is capitalised, along with any proper noun in it. Title case is English and is an error in Swedish.\n\nA greeting line ends with an exclamation mark or with nothing at all: *Hej Susanne!*, *Hej Susanne*. The comma of *Hej Susanne,* is the English convention and reads as imported. A closing takes no comma either — *Med vänlig hälsning* stands on its own line, and the name stands on the next.\n\nTwo forms both listed in *Svenska Akademiens ordlista* are both established Swedish, neither of them the error: *i dag* and *idag*, *ska* and *skall*, *över huvud taget* and *överhuvudtaget*."

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

Klart. Enda korrigeringsrundan förkastades, så texten kommer tillbaka orörd och alla fynd står kvar olösta.

**Inställningar:** genre `opinion` (från anropet), språk `sv` (från anropet). Ingen teknik används, eftersom opinion-genren anger att den normalt skrivs utan teknik. Ingen brief valdes.

````markdown
# Kommunledningen hatar människor

Sanna Ek, Öppna beslut

Kommunstyrelsen borde behålla telefonbokning under ett halvårs försök i alla sju lokaler. Alla vet att politikerna vill stänga ute äldre för att spara miljoner.

## Bakgrund

Det gjordes 96 bokningar på webben och 24 via telefon. Det bevisar att 20 procent av kommunens invånare inte kan använda internet. Kommunens pilotrapport från den 8 april 2026 säger samtidigt att bokningarna inte räknar unika personer och att digital vana inte undersöktes.

## Diskussion

Förvaltningen invänder att dubbla kanaler innebär dubbel administration. Handlingarna saknar tidsmätning. Därför kostar det ingenting att behålla telefonbokningen. Föreningen vill att förvaltningen mäter tidsåtgång och frågar användarna varför de väljer en bokningsväg. Försökets kostnad är inte beräknad.

Nu är det dags att agera.
````

## Fynd – alla olösta

1. **Rubriken ”Kommunledningen hatar människor”** påstår något texten inte säger och ger motparten ett motiv som ingenting i texten stöder. Ordet ”kommunledningen” finns inte heller i brödtexten. En läsare som bara ser rubriken tror att texten handlar om kommunledningens känslor. Läsaren får inte veta vad texten driver: att telefonbokningen ska behållas under ett halvårsförsök. Tonen är dessutom mycket högre än i resten av texten.
2. **Ingress saknas.** Artikelanatomin kräver en fristående ingress mellan rubrik och byline, och mätskriptet anger den som frånvarande. En saknad del skrivs inte vid en granskning. Den lämnas åt en person att fylla i.
3. **”Alla vet att politikerna vill stänga ute äldre för att spara miljoner.”** Meningen stöder sig på en tom auktoritet (”alla vet”) och tillskriver politikerna ett motiv texten saknar belägg för. Texten säger ingenting om äldre. ”Miljoner” motsägs av textens egen uppgift att försökets kostnad inte är beräknad.
4. **”Det bevisar att 20 procent av kommunens invånare inte kan använda internet.”** Slutsatsen håller inte. 24 av 120 är 20 procent av bokningarna, inte av invånarna. Meningen därefter säger dessutom att bokningarna inte räknar unika personer och att digital vana inte undersöktes. Den meningen avgränsar vad texten kan påstå och ska stå kvar.
5. **”Därför kostar det ingenting att behålla telefonbokningen.”** Att handlingarna saknar tidsmätning visar inte att kostnaden är noll. Samma stycke säger att försökets kostnad inte är beräknad. Förvaltningens invändning bemöts alltså med en slutsats som texten själv motsäger.
6. **”Föreningen vill …”**: ingen förening har presenterats i brödtexten. Bylinen nämner Öppna beslut, men texten säger inte att det är den föreningen som avses. Läsaren vet inte vem som ställer kravet. Det går inte att rätta utan en uppgift som saknas i texten.
7. **Mellanrubrikerna ”Bakgrund” och ”Diskussion”** är rena etiketter som kunde stå i vilken text som helst. I en debattartikel ska mellanrubrikerna bära argumentet. Den som skummar får inte veta vad avsnitten säger, till exempel att var femte bokning gjordes via telefon eller att tidsåtgången inte är mätt.
8. **Slutet ”Nu är det dags att agera.”** nämner ingen handling och ingen som ska agera. Raden står dessutom sist i ett avsnitt som för argumentet, men avslutningen ska vara ett eget avsnitt med egen mellanrubrik. Förslaget att kommunstyrelsen behåller telefonbokningen under försöket finns redan i inledningen och kan göras till uppmaningen.
9. **Siffrorna 96 och 24 och ”alla sju lokaler”** saknar källa och tidsperiod, och det framgår inte vad som bokas. Läsaren kan därför inte bedöma underlaget. Det går inte att rätta utan uppgifter som saknas i texten.

## Förkastad korrigeringsrunda

Korrigeringsbudgeten på en runda gick åt. Rundan skrev om rubriken till ”Behåll telefonbokningen ett halvår och mät tidsåtgången” och gav slutet ett eget avsnitt, ”Kommunstyrelsen och förvaltningen har var sitt steg att ta”. Där stod bland annat att ”Förvaltningen kan mäta tidsåtgången och fråga användarna”. Den ändringen skapade ett nytt fel: föreningens krav på mätning blev skribentens egen uppmaning, både i rubriken och i slutet. Texten visar inte att skribenten står bakom kravet (se fynd 6), och att inte invända mot ett krav är inte detsamma som att ställa sig bakom det.
